advisor.summary: §179 is first-year expensing with precision: an election, made asset by asset and dollar by dollar on Form 4562, to deduct qualifying tangible personal property — and, under §179(f), roofs, HVAC, fire protection, and security systems on nonresidential buildings — in the placed-in-service year. For 2026 the ceiling is $2,560,000, phasing out dollar-for-dollar once total §179 property placed in service passes $4,090,000 (OBBBA-raised and indexed). Two limits govern every election: the deduction cannot exceed aggregate active-business taxable income under §179(b)(3) (the excess carries forward), and for pass-throughs both the dollar and income limits apply at the entity and again at the owner. With 100% bonus back as the volume tool, §179's remaining edge is selectivity — landing a taxable-income target exactly, and reaching building components bonus cannot touch. The engine models the elected amount as a current business deduction.
mechanics: The election works asset by asset: on Form 4562 the taxpayer can expense one asset in full, half of another, and depreciate the remainder — unlike bonus under §168(k), which is all-or-nothing by class.

Eligible property under §179(d) covers tangible personal property used in an active trade or business, off-the-shelf software, and qualified real property under §179(f) — roofs, HVAC, fire protection and alarm, and security systems on nonresidential buildings, 39-year property that bonus cannot expense.
The 2026 dollar limit is $2,560,000, reduced dollar-for-dollar once total §179 property placed in service tops $4,090,000 — a phase-out aimed at genuinely large acquisition years.
§179(b)(3) caps the deduction at aggregate active-business taxable income (W-2 wages count toward the base); the disallowed excess carries forward indefinitely rather than vanishing.
For S corporations and partnerships, the limits apply twice — at the entity and again at each owner — and the deduction passes through separately stated.
Recapture under §179(d)(10) applies if business use falls to 50% or below during the recovery period.

authority.note: The expensing election plus the 2026 dollar limit and phase-out structure, as raised by OBBBA and indexed.
The taxable-income limitation: capped at aggregate active-business income, with indefinite carryforward of the excess.
The eligible-property definition, the purchase requirement, qualified real property (roofs, HVAC, fire/alarm, security on nonresidential buildings), and the (d)(10) recapture rule.
The bonus alternative — the benchmark every §179 election is weighed against.
Part I is where the election and the asset-by-asset amounts are reported on a timely filed return.

requirements: Qualifying property placed in service during the year in an active trade or business — not a mere investment activity.
Aggregate active-business taxable income at least equal to the intended deduction, or a deliberate acceptance of the carryforward.
Total §179 property below the phase-out ceiling to keep the full limit.
Business use above 50%, maintained throughout the recovery period.
risks: The signature misfire is electing §179 on rental-property assets: most rental real estate is not an active trade or business for §179 purposes, and the disallowance is mechanical — put the analysis in the file before the election, not in the response to a notice; no marquee case governs because the statute does the work.
An election above the income limit produces a carryforward, not savings — pointless where bonus would deduct currently.
Owners aggregating §179 from multiple entities can hit the owner-level cap without warning.
A drop in business use to 50% or below triggers recapture at ordinary rates.
Several states impose lower §179 ceilings and require addbacks, so the state deduction can diverge sharply from the federal one.
stateNotes: Conformity: state §179 conformity is messier than bonus — several states cap the deduction at their own lower limits with addback and recovery schedules; screen the footprint before promising a combined rate.
Missouri conforms to the federal §179 limits through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121), with no separate Missouri cap.

PTET interaction: §179 passes through separately stated while the PTET is computed on entity income — confirm the state’s PTET base treats separately stated §179 consistently before projecting the credit.
reviewChecklist: Every elected asset confirmed as active-trade-or-business property — rental-side assets specifically screened.
The §179(b)(3) income limit computed at entity and owner level before amounts are set.
Election coordinated with bonus: §179 for the targeted dollars and reachable building components, bonus for the volume.
Listed-property business-use percentages documented and recapture exposure calendared.
Form 4562 amounts tie out to the fixed-asset additions schedule.

client.teaser: Choose exactly which purchases to write off now — down to the dollar.
client.headline: Write off equipment the year you buy it — on your terms
plainEnglish: When your business buys equipment, computers, or even a new roof or HVAC for a commercial building, the normal rule spreads the deduction over many years. A special election lets you deduct the cost right away, up to a very large yearly limit.

What sets this election apart is control. You pick which purchases to write off now and which to spread out — dollar by dollar. That lets us land your taxable income right where it saves you the most.
It also reaches things other fast write-off rules miss, like certain building parts on commercial property. We use it alongside the other rules, each where it works best.
client.analogy: It is a dimmer switch for deductions, not an on-off switch — we dial in the exact amount that fits your year.
benefits: Deduct qualifying purchases right away, up to the annual limit
You pick the assets and amounts — precise control of timing
Reaches used equipment and certain commercial building upgrades
steps: WE review everything the business placed in service this year.
WE compute the amount that saves the most — not just the maximum.
WE make the election on your return; there is nothing separate to file.
YOU keep the assets in business use — heavy personal use can claw the deduction back.
clientCommitments: Tell us about large purchases before year-end
Keep business-use records for vehicles and shared-use equipment

annualMaintenance: Coordinate §179 elections with bonus depreciation before each filing
Track business-use percentages on listed property
Monitor carryforwards created by the income limit
deliverables: Asset-by-asset election schedule with savings analysis
Form 4562 filing reflecting the chosen amounts
Recapture-exposure log for the client file
